Filters

  • Filters

      • Environment and protocol
    • Lua filters
      • Requirements
      • Writing a Lua filter

Apex supports AST-level filters that operate on a Pandoc-compatible JSON representation of the document, similar to Pandoc filters.

Filters let you:

  • Walk and transform the document structure (blocks and inlines) in any language.
  • Apply custom formatting rules, content checks, or structural changes.
  • Reuse existing Pandoc JSON filter ecosystems (Python, Ruby, Node, etc.).

Under the hood, Apex:

  1. Parses Markdown using cmark-gfm into its internal AST.
  2. Converts that AST to a Pandoc-style JSON AST.
  3. Pipes the JSON through one or more external filters.
  4. Parses the transformed JSON back into a cmark AST and renders to HTML. 
markdown  →  cmark AST  →  Pandoc JSON  →  filters  →  Pandoc JSON  →  cmark AST  →  HTML

Enabling filters

Filters are configured via the Apex CLI:

  • --filter NAME

    • Run a single filter from your user filters directory:
      • $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/apex/filters/NAME, or
      • ~/.config/apex/filters/NAME (on macOS/Linux when XDG is not set).
    • NAME should be an executable script/binary that implements the Pandoc JSON filter contract.

  • --filters

    • Run all executable files in the filters directory, sorted by name.
    • Useful for assembling a standard filter pipeline (e.g. 01-title, 10-delink, etc.).

  • --lua-filter FILE

    • Run a Lua script as an AST filter via the system lua interpreter.
    • Internally Apex invokes lua "FILE" as a JSON filter, so your script should read a Pandoc JSON document from stdin and write JSON to stdout.

  • --no-strict-filters

    • By default, filters are strict:
      • If a filter exits with a non-zero status or produces invalid JSON, Apex aborts the conversion with an error.
    • With --no-strict-filters, Apex:
      • Logs a warning and skips the failing filter,
      • Continues processing with the previous AST.

Environment and protocol

Each filter is executed as a separate process:

  • Input:

    • Apex writes a single Pandoc JSON document to the filter’s stdin.
    • This document has:
      • pandoc-api-version field,
      • meta (document metadata),
      • blocks (list of block elements).

  • Output:

    • The filter writes a (possibly transformed) Pandoc JSON document to stdout.
    • Apex uses the result as the input AST for the next filter, or for rendering.

This is identical in spirit to Pandoc’s JSON filter model (Pandoc filters), so libraries like pandocfilters (Python) or various language ports work unchanged.

Lua filters

--lua-filter FILE runs a Lua script as an AST filter. Apex invokes the system lua interpreter with the script path; the script receives a Pandoc JSON document on stdin and must write a (possibly transformed) Pandoc JSON document to stdout. No Pandoc-specific Lua runtime is required.

Requirements

  • A Lua interpreter on your PATH (lua, lua5.1, lua5.2, lua5.3, or lua5.4).
  • A JSON library for Lua (e.g. dkjson), since Lua has no built-in JSON support. Install dkjson with LuaRocks: 
    brew install luarocks    # macOS/Homebrew
luarocks install dkjson

Writing a Lua filter

  1. Read the full document from stdin (e.g. in 4KB chunks and concatenate).
  2. Decode the JSON (e.g. dkjson.decode).
  3. Walk and transform the blocks (and optionally meta) as needed. Block and inline objects use t (type) and c (content); Apex accepts keys in any order (e.g. "c" before "t" as emitted by dkjson).
  4. Encode the result back to JSON and write it to stdout (e.g. dkjson.encode).

Minimal example 

local json = require("dkjson")

local input = io.read("*a")
local doc = json.decode(input)
if not doc then
  io.stderr:write("Invalid JSON\n")
  os.exit(1)
end

-- Optional: transform doc.blocks or doc.meta
-- doc.blocks = ...

io.write(json.encode(doc))

Use it: 

apex --lua-filter myfilter.lua input.md > output.html

For a full example that rewrites blocks (e.g. unwrapping paragraphs into raw HTML), see the apex-filter-unwrap repository.

User filter directory

On macOS/Linux, Apex looks for filters in:

  • $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/apex/filters (if set), or
  • ~/.config/apex/filters

Use apex --list-filters to see installed filters and those available from the apex-filters directory; use apex --install-filter ID and apex --uninstall-filter ID to install or remove a filter by ID. See Command-Line Options for details.

Each filter is just an executable file in that directory: 

~/.config/apex/filters/
  title        # Ruby script
  delink       # Python script
  ...

Example: Title filter (Ruby)

This filter:

  • Reads a Pandoc JSON document from stdin.
  • Reads meta.title.
  • If the first block is not already an H1, prepends a Header 1 with the title. 
#!/usr/bin/env ruby

require "json"

doc = JSON.parse($stdin.read)
blocks = doc["blocks"] || []
meta   = doc["meta"]   || {}

title_text = nil

if meta.key?("title")
  t = meta["title"]
  case t["t"]
  when "MetaString"
    title_text = t["c"].to_s
  when "MetaInlines", "MetaText"
    inlines = t["c"] || []
    title_text = inlines.map { |inline|
      inline.is_a?(Hash) && inline["t"] == "Str" ? inline["c"].to_s : nil
    }.compact.join(" ")
  end
end

if title_text && !title_text.strip.empty?
  first = blocks.first
  already_h1 =
    first &&
    first["t"] == "Header" &&
    first["c"].is_a?(Array) &&
    first["c"][0] == 1

  unless already_h1
    header = {
      "t" => "Header",
      "c" => [
        1,
        ["", [], []],
        [{ "t" => "Str", "c" => title_text }]
      ]
    }
    blocks.unshift(header)
    doc["blocks"] = blocks
  end
end

puts JSON.dump(doc)

Install and use: 

mkdir -p ~/.config/apex/filters
cp title.rb ~/.config/apex/filters/title
chmod +x ~/.config/apex/filters/title

apex --filter title input.md > output.html

Example: Delink filter (Python)

This filter:

  • Finds Link inlines:
    • { "t": "Link", "c": [Attr, [Inlines...], [url, title]] }
  • Replaces them with Span inlines that keep only the text:
    • { "t": "Span", "c": [Attr, [Inlines...]] } 
#!/usr/bin/env python3

import json
import sys

def delink(node):
  if isinstance(node, dict) and node.get("t") == "Link":
    c = node.get("c", [])
    if isinstance(c, list) and len(c) == 3:
      attr, inlines, _target = c
      return {"t": "Span", "c": [attr, inlines]}
  return node

def walk(x):
  x = delink(x)
  if isinstance(x, dict):
    return {k: walk(v) for k, v in x.items()}
  if isinstance(x, list):
    return [walk(i) for i in x]
  return x

def main():
  data = json.loads(sys.stdin.read())
  data = walk(data)
  json.dump(data, sys.stdout)

if __name__ == "__main__":
  main()

Install and use: 

mkdir -p ~/.config/apex/filters
cp delink.py ~/.config/apex/filters/delink
chmod +x ~/.config/apex/filters/delink

apex --filter delink input.md > output.html

Multiple filters and ordering

You can compose filters in two ways:

  • Multiple --filter flags: 

    apex --filter title --filter delink input.md > output.html

    Filters run in the order they appear on the command line.

  • --filters directory mode: 

    apex --filters input.md > output.html

    All executable files in the filters directory are run in sorted filename order. You can control order via prefixes like 01-title, 10-delink, etc.

You can also combine both: 

apex --filters --filter extra input.md > output.html

Directory filters run first, followed by explicit --filter commands.

Relationship to plugins

Filters are AST-level and operate on Pandoc JSON between parse and render.

Plugins are:

  • String-level pre-parse or post-render transformations.
  • Configured via plugin manifests and run through the plugin system (see Plugins).

Use filters when you need structured transformations of the document tree or want to reuse Pandoc JSON filter tooling; use plugins when a simpler string pass (regex, external formatter, etc.) is enough.
